summary:
Kahramanmaraş province operates under Turkish national law, and the source inventory records no Kahramanmaraş-specific statute, incident, or court case concerning trans people. What a trans visitor faces in the province is the national framework as it functions elsewhere in Türkiye, which is documented as a structured and deliberate state campaign against LGBT people rather than residual prejudice.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal code to imprison for up to three years anyone who incites or promotes conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, criminalise participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with penalties of up to four years, and restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under a requirement of permanent infertility, exposing providers to fines and up to seven years and patients to up to three years in prison. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected. The package is national legislation and would apply in Kahramanmaraş; it had not been enacted when reported.

Enforcement has run ahead of the statute. In Istanbul's Beyoğlu district on 31 July 2025, police detained trans women for identity checks, recording their names and filming videos of the stops. That incident falls outside Kahramanmaraş, but it evidences national practice: identity-document checks are used against trans people on the street and in commercial premises, with detentions for background-check purposes and no charge required. Türkiye also requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and detention warnings for non-compliance. For a visitor whose appearance does not match the passport gender marker, every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which presentation and documents are compared.

Kaos GL's 2025 record, A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People, counts 313 liberty violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the previous year, mostly detentions, alongside 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 and mostly linked to peaceful assembly, and six right-to-life violations of which three were recorded as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. Because the Turkish state keeps no hate-crime statistics, these figures are compiled from media and civil-society reporting. The same documentation describes hostility institutionalised under instructions to public institutions for an officially designated Year of the Family, hate speech from senior officials, and artistic events cancelled or banned. These describe national practice, not a provincial choice, and the source records no Kahramanmaraş-specific finding.

Two further national layers bear on a visitor's exposure. Prisoners are placed by registered sex, so trans people are held in gendered facilities that do not correspond to their gender, with arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement, and restricted healthcare documented by the Prison Insider country profile. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording an 'other' option and required electronic reports, which risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
The Turkish government's stated justification for the legislative package is protection of the family and public morals, language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma. The draft was pending when reported, and its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions already bind them; the Beyoğlu detentions of July 2025 illustrate enforcement preceding enactment.

The scale of the national documentation is the main comparative marker available for the province. Kaos GL recorded 299 detention decisions in 2025, of which 43 were taken off the record, and the total volume of liberty violations at roughly two and a half times the 2024 figure. Counts of violence are compiled by civil society because the state maintains no hate-crime statistics, so official figures understate the risk, and trans people are recorded as the group most affected by the killings.

Kahramanmaraş is a province, not a distinct legal regime. The absence of a named Kahramanmaraş incident in the inventory is a gap in reporting rather than evidence of local tolerance; the sources used here are national in scope and count violations from media and civil-society material, which concentrates coverage on major cities.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than seventy interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the depth of the pattern, not as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Residents who are read as LGBT face routine police identity checks in which names are recorded and video is taken, and the resulting records persist after release. Kaos GL's documentation attributes the increase in detentions to instructions issued to public institutions under the Year of the Family designation, so the pressure is administrative as well as penal.

Detention totals include 43 decisions taken off the record in 2025 alongside 256 recorded through formal channels, meaning a substantial share of liberty violations leave no official trace. Complaints by detainees are documented as ineffective and capable of attracting further violence.

Trans prisoners are assigned according to registered sex, including trans men held in women's facilities, and LGBT detainees are managed through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement, with arbitrary body and strip searches, restricted hospital transfer, and transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks. There is no staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners and the administration operates on a binary basis.

Transition-related care is narrowing. The Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular adding gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, and the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation requiring electronic reports and barring the 'other' option, place trans patients into identifiable categories in official health records, with the draft judicial package proposing to confine such care to people aged 25 and over under permanent infertility.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kahramanmaraş-specific statute, police incident, detention, or court case concerning trans people is recorded in the source inventory. Provincial-level conditions, including whether police in Kahramanmaraş conduct identity-check detentions of the kind documented in Istanbul, are unresolved and not sourced here.

The July 2025 identity-check detentions described in the sources occurred in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district and are reported as national practice, not as a Kahramanmaraş event.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted, amended, or abandoned since it was reported on 29 October 2025 is unresolved in the inventory.

The inventory does not establish whether health facilities in Kahramanmaraş apply circulars of the kind issued by the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate, nor whether gender-affirming care is available locally under current rules.
